cells.tense: You are carrying what there is to carry and pointing somewhere at the same time, right now.
cells.ask: Tell one person the direction you're moving in. Then hold steady while they take it in.
cells.core:
Something has settled. You know which light you're moving toward, and you're carrying what it costs to move. The weight hasn't bent you and your bearing has kept. That's the shape of it working: you decide the direction, and the strength you keep is the reason it can be a direction instead of a wish.

Carrying and choosing are one act here, not two. You can stay in contact with what's heavy and still point somewhere. Next time it's tested — and it will be — the thing to feed is simple: put the direction in front of someone. Not for approval. Because a direction said out loud is one you can keep.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying it and steering by it at once.
cells.verb: picking the light you move toward instead of the one handed to you
cells.place: where you hold your shape under weight without going hard

cells.tense: You are braced for a weight that hasn't arrived and may not be yours to hold.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding ahead of time and set it down until someone actually hands it to you.
cells.core:
Before anyone asks, you're braced. The shape of what's coming has already been taken on, and the strength that would hold today's weight is going into a future you can't write in yet. This feels like readiness. It isn't. It's holding a door shut that nobody is knocking on.

Here's what the strain is doing: it's making the direction harder to see, not clearer. When everything ahead is a load to bear, no light looks worth moving toward. The way back runs through not-knowing — letting one thing stay undecided, letting a question sit without an answer you've rehearsed. Comfort with that is what your perceptions land on. Set one thing down. See what's actually in your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying tomorrow's weight today, and it costs you the direction.

cells.tense: You can still see the light, and you are standing still where the ground holds you.
cells.ask: Name one direction out loud — to anyone, even in a note to yourself — then do one small thing today that only makes sense if it's true.
cells.core:
The light is still there. You can see it when you're not asking much of yourself, but the strength to move toward it isn't around right now. So the direction goes unnamed. Not because you don't know. Because carrying anything at all feels like too much to ask.

The gap isn't in what you know. It's in what you can hold. And that doesn't come back by trying harder at it — it comes back sideways, through small care that doesn't exhaust you. Tend something. Let one thing grow without you gripping it. Strength refills from small care, not from the demand. Naming a direction is the first small thing; the rest follows from there.
cells.sheetLine: You can still see the light. You just can't hold it up.

cells.tense: You are already steering by something and calling it just how things are.
cells.ask: Say 'this is mine' about one direction you've been calling obvious or inevitable.
cells.core:
You've been setting the direction for a while now — it shows in what you choose, what you refuse, which way you turn when nobody's asking you to turn. But you describe it as if the direction were finding itself. The steering is running. The ownership isn't.

That costs you. A bearing you don't claim gets revised by whoever's loudest, and your own strength goes to defending ground you didn't say was yours. The fix is smaller than it sounds: take one thing you've been treating as obvious and say plainly that you chose it. Not to announce it. To have it. Strength gets easier once the hand on the wheel is named.
